questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: What Peer Review Does and Does Not Do
questions.learningObjective: Identify what peer review can and cannot guarantee about a study
questions.stem: An amateur astronomer logs that a journal accepted her paper after peer review, so she concludes the data are flawless. Which belief is mistaken?

options.text: Peer review checks plausibility and method, not truth of every datum
Peer review guarantees the findings will replicate in a new sample
options.misconception: treats acceptance as proof of reproducibility

options.text: Peer review confirms the data were collected exactly as reported
options.misconception: confuses editorial review with data auditing

options.text: Peer review removes all possibility of researcher bias
options.misconception: assumes reviewers can detect every bias

questions.explanation: Peer review evaluates method, reasoning, and fit, but it cannot verify raw data or guarantee replication. The tempting idea that acceptance equals truth overstates what review does.
questions.hint: Review checks method, not every number.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize selective reporting as a threat to validity
questions.stem: A beekeeper's logbook inspired astronomer Kael runs five analyses and posts only the one with p<.05. What is the main problem?

options.text: The sample size is too small for any of the analyses
The reported result may be a chance finding amplified by selection
All five analyses were probably correct anyway
Peer reviewers will always catch and remove the extra analyses

questions.explanation: Choosing among many analyses and reporting only the significant one inflates false positives. The other options misplace blame on sample size, assume all tests are valid, or overstate review.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: The Comparison Group
questions.learningObjective: Justify the need for a comparison group
questions.stem: An astronomer gives all volunteers a new meditation app and finds calmer logs. Explain why a comparison group is still needed.

answer.exemplar: Without a comparison group we cannot know whether calmness came from the app, the season, or expectation. A control group that does not use the app isolates the app's effect and rules out those alternatives.

questions.explanation: A single-group pre-post change may reflect time, season, or placebo effects rather than the treatment. A comparison group provides the counterfactual needed to attribute change to the app.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a double-blind design
questions.stem: In an astronomer's study, neither participants nor the staff recording star counts know who got the real supplement. What design is this?

options.text: Double-blind: both participants and staff are unaware
Single-blind: only participants are unaware of condition
Open-label: everyone knows the condition
Triple-blind: only the statistician is aware

questions.explanation: When both participants and data-collecting staff are unaware of condition, the study is double-blind. Single-blind leaves staff aware, open-label removes blinding, and triple-blind is not required here.

questions.learningObjective: Describe experimenter expectancy effects
questions.stem: An astronomer expects her new filter to improve vision and unconsciously records better scores for that group. What threat does this create?

options.text: Demand characteristics from participants guessing the hypothesis
A ceiling effect making all scores identical
Random error that cancels out across many trials
Experimenter expectancy biasing measurement and results

questions.explanation: The researcher's expectation can shape recording and behavior, biasing outcomes. Demand characteristics involve participants, random error does not systematically favor one group, and ceiling effects are unrelated.

questions.stem: Design a study so an astronomer cannot quietly swap outcomes after seeing data. What single step best prevents this?

questions.learningObjective: Detect a floor effect in a measure
questions.stem: An astronomer's error-count measure bottoms out at zero for most novices, so training effects are invisible. What is this called?

options.text: A ceiling effect from scores clustering at the top
A practice effect from repeated testing
A floor effect from scores clustering at the minimum
A regression artifact from extreme initial scores

questions.explanation: When scores pile at the minimum, improvements cannot show, which is a floor effect. Ceiling is the opposite, practice effects involve learning, and regression is a different phenomenon.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a mitigation for experimenter bias
questions.stem: To curb an astronomer's influence on results, which procedure is most direct?

options.text: Use standardized scripts and blinded assessment
Increase the sample size to wash out bias
Tell participants the hypothesis openly
Let the researcher choose the outcome after data collection

questions.explanation: Standardized scripts and blinded assessment directly reduce experimenter influence. Larger N does not remove systematic bias, disclosing the hypothesis raises demand effects, and post-hoc outcome choice invites cherry-picking.

questions.stem: An astronomer must pick an outcome to detect a small training effect. Which choice best supports detection?

options.text: A measure already near its maximum for most participants

A measure with mid-range scores and room to move
A measure that only records pass or fail

questions.explanation: An outcome with mid-range scores and headroom can reveal small gains. Measures near the ceiling, lacking units, or binary pass-fail are less sensitive to change.

questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: The Comparison Group
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a waitlist control is useful
questions.stem: An astronomer uses a waitlist control that receives treatment later. Explain its advantage.

answer.exemplar: A waitlist control eventually gets the treatment, addressing fairness while still providing a no-treatment comparison during the study period. This supports causal inference without denying access.

questions.explanation: Waitlist controls balance ethics and inference by delaying treatment. They still provide a comparison period before treatment begins.
questions.hint: Delayed treatment balances ethics and inference.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: Who Knows Which Condition
questions.learningObjective: Identify the condition assignment in a single-blind study
questions.stem: In a single-blind astronomer's study, who is unaware of condition assignment?

options.text: The researchers recording outcomes
Everyone involved in the study
The statistician analyzing data
The participants receiving treatment

questions.explanation: Single-blind means participants are unaware of their condition. Staff, statisticians, or everyone being unaware describes other designs.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: What the Investigator Expects
questions.learningObjective: Identify a sign of expectancy bias
questions.stem: An astronomer's own ratings favor her hypothesis group, while blinded ratings do not. What does this suggest?

options.text: Expectancy bias in the unblinded ratings
The blinded ratings are simply less accurate
Random error in the blinded ratings
A ceiling effect in both rating sets

questions.explanation: Divergence between unblinded and blinded ratings suggests expectancy bias. Dismissing the safeguard, blaming random error, or invoking ceiling effects are weaker explanations.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: What Peer Review Does and Does Not Do
questions.learningObjective: State a limitation regarding generalizability
questions.stem: An astronomer's peer-reviewed sample is 12 volunteers from one club. What limitation remains despite review?

options.text: Review guarantees the sample is representative
The findings are certainly false
Generalizability to broader populations is limited
Peer review caused the small sample

questions.explanation: Review does not ensure representativeness, so generalizability remains limited. It does not guarantee representativeness, prove falsity, or cause small samples.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: Reporting Only the Analyses That Worked
questions.learningObjective: Recommend a transparency practice
questions.stem: An astronomer wants readers to verify her selective-reporting claim. What practice best enables this?

answer.exemplar: Share the full dataset and analysis code in a repository, plus a preregistration. Readers can then reproduce all analyses and check for undisclosed selections.

questions.explanation: Open data and code let others reproduce analyses and detect undisclosed selections. Without them, selective reporting stays hidden.
questions.hint: Open data and code enable verification.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: The Variable Set and the Variable Measured
questions.learningObjective: Identify a latent variable
questions.stem: An astronomer measures several questionnaire items to index an unobserved trait like curiosity. What is curiosity here?

options.text: An observed dependent variable
A confounding variable to remove
An independent variable manipulated
A latent variable inferred from indicators

questions.explanation: Curiosity is a latent variable inferred from observed items. It is not directly observed, manipulated, or a confound to remove.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: Choosing an Outcome That Can Move
questions.learningObjective: Compute a percent change in an outcome
questions.stem: An astronomer's alertness score rises from 80 to 100. What is the percent increase?
questions.explanation: The increase is 20 on a base of 80, so 20/80=0.25 or 25 percent. Using 100 as the base would be wrong.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: Degrees of Freedom in a Three-Group Comparison
questions.learningObjective: State between-groups df formula
questions.stem: In a one-way ANOVA, between-groups degrees of freedom equals what?

options.text: Number of groups minus one
Total participants minus one
Total participants minus groups
Number of groups plus one

questions.explanation: Between-groups df is groups minus one. Total participants minus one gives total df, participants minus groups gives within df, and adding one is incorrect.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: The Comparison Group
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of a placebo control
questions.stem: An astronomer gives a sham lens to the control group. What is the main purpose?

options.text: To increase the sample size
To provide no comparison at all
To match the ritual and expectation of treatment
To eliminate the need for randomization

questions.explanation: A placebo matches ritual and expectation, isolating the active ingredient's effect. It does not remove comparison, increase N, or replace randomization.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: Who Knows Which Condition
questions.learningObjective: Identify triple-blind design
questions.stem: In an astronomer's study, participants, staff, and analysts are all unaware of condition. What is this?

options.text: Single-blind with only participants unaware
Double-blind with participants and staff unaware
Open-label with full disclosure
Triple-blind with all three roles unaware

questions.explanation: When participants, staff, and analysts are all unaware, the design is triple-blind. Single and double blind cover fewer roles, and open-label discloses everything.
questions.hint: All three roles unaware is triple-blind.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: What the Investigator Expects
questions.learningObjective: Recommend a design to reduce expectancy
questions.stem: An astronomer wants to minimize her influence on star-count outcomes. Which combination is best?

options.text: Larger sample with the same unblinded rater
Choosing the outcome after data collection
Disclosing the hypothesis to participants
Blinded rater plus standardized protocol

questions.explanation: A blinded rater and standardized protocol directly reduce expectancy influence. Larger N, disclosure, or post-hoc outcome choice do not.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: What Peer Review Does and Does Not Do
questions.learningObjective: State what review cannot do
questions.stem: An astronomer believes peer review proves her theory true. Explain why this overstates review.

answer.exemplar: Peer review only judges whether the work meets standards of method and argument; it does not verify truth or guarantee future replication. Proof requires independent replication and continued testing.

questions.explanation: Review evaluates standards, not truth. Replication and further testing are needed for stronger claims.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: Reporting Only the Analyses That Worked
questions.learningObjective: Define selective outcome reporting
questions.stem: An astronomer measures five outcomes but publishes only the significant one. What is this?

options.text: Selective outcome reporting
Preregistration of all outcomes
Bonferroni correction
Power analysis

questions.explanation: Publishing only significant outcomes among many is selective outcome reporting. Preregistration, Bonferroni correction, and power analysis are safeguards.
questions.hint: Publishing only winners is selective reporting.

questions.learningObjective: Identify an extraneous variable
questions.stem: Room temperature varies across an astronomer's sessions and could affect alertness scores. What is temperature here?

options.text: The independent variable of interest
The dependent variable outcome
An extraneous variable to control
A latent construct of interest

questions.explanation: Temperature is an extraneous variable that could affect outcomes and should be controlled. It is not the IV of interest, the DV, or a latent construct.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Foundations of Psychology: Choosing an Outcome That Can Move
questions.learningObjective: Compute a standardized gain
questions.stem: An astronomer's mean gain is 4 points on a measure with SD 8. What is the standardized gain?
questions.explanation: Standardized gain is mean gain divided by SD: 4/8=0.5. Dividing by variance would be wrong.
